paragraphs: AutoMoT addresses a practical challenge in autonomous driving: combining a model’s understanding of a scene with the actions needed to drive through it. Existing integration approaches can leave reasoning and action representations poorly aligned, use too little of a pretrained model’s reasoning ability, or introduce delays when producing driving actions.

The proposed system brings reasoning and action generation into one vision-language-action model. Its mixture-of-transformers architecture shares attention within corresponding layers, connecting the tasks while supporting asynchronous inference. Different tasks can therefore run at different frequencies. This matters because the system can coordinate reasoning and control without requiring every task to execute on the same schedule. The authors also investigate a diffusion-based action refiner to improve driving performance through additional fine-tuning.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks in both open- and closed-loop evaluation. The paper also studies when driving-specific fine-tuning is needed and how much it helps, examining the extent to which pretrained vision-language capabilities carry over to driving.
icml-2026-automot-a-unified-vision-langu.tldr: AutoMoT combines scene reasoning and driving actions in one model that runs different tasks asynchronously.

paragraphs: This paper starts by analytically solving Mountain Car, a standard reinforcement learning control problem. An optimal solution gives the authors a reference for measuring how closely learned agents approach the best possible behavior. Their analysis finds that the optimal control is relatively simple, while modern reinforcement learning agents still fall substantially short of it.

Motivated by that result, the authors introduce Chebyshev policies as an alternative representation for control decisions. They establish that this policy class is universal in the sense of being dense, and show that it can replace neural networks within existing training methods. The goal is to represent effective low-dimensional control with far fewer adjustable parameters, supporting sample efficiency, interpretability, and real-time use.

The reported comparison reduces regret by a factor of 6.18 while using 277 times fewer parameters. Evaluations extend to other reinforcement learning tasks and a real nonlinear motion-control testbed. Across these evaluations, Chebyshev policies improve performance with PPO, ARS, and REINFORCE, supporting their usefulness for low-dimensional control.
icml-2026-chebyshev-policies-and-the-mou.tldr: An analytical Mountain Car solution motivates compact Chebyshev policies that outperform neural-network policies in the reported low-dimensional control evaluations.

paragraphs: ConceptMoE addresses the mismatch between uniform computation per token and the differing difficulty of text sequences. Some stretches are easy to predict, while others require more reasoning. The method learns to group semantically similar tokens into larger units called concepts, with a target compression ratio controlling how much the sequence is shortened.

The authors use a mixture-of-experts architecture to examine whether this change helps independently of model size or total computation. They redistribute the computation saved by compression so that comparisons match baseline FLOPs and parameter counts. This makes the evaluation informative about the architecture itself, rather than simply about spending more resources.

ConceptMoE reports improvements of 0.9 points in language pretraining, 2.3 in long-context tasks, and 0.6 in multimodal tasks. Conversion through continual training with layer looping gains 5.5 points. At a compression ratio of two, attention computation falls fourfold and the key-value cache halves. Reported speedups reach 175% for prefill and 117% for decoding, combining quality gains with reduced processing demands.
icml-2026-conceptmoe-adaptive-token-to-c.tldr: ConceptMoE learns to compress tokens into concepts, improving reported task performance while reducing attention and cache costs.

paragraphs: Learning a continuous-variable Hamiltonian means identifying the coefficients that describe a quantum system’s dynamics from noisy measurements. The system can have an infinite-dimensional state space even when only finitely many coefficients need to be recovered. Existing protocols with Heisenberg-limited scaling face restrictions involving low-order structure, noise sensitivity, or generalization to multiple modes.

The proposed Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation protocol actively organizes data acquisition using predetermined probes and number-preserving transformations. These operations turn finite-order bosonic Hamiltonian learning into a polynomial recovery problem. That reformulation connects the quantum measurement task to a more structured coefficient-estimation problem. For multiple modes, the authors develop a hierarchical recovery procedure with better statistical efficiency than estimating all coefficients simultaneously.

The paper proves Heisenberg-limited scaling of total evolution time together with robustness to state-preparation and measurement errors. It also extends the method to coefficient learning for first-quantized Hamiltonians. Numerical experiments on nonlinear systems with one or multiple modes reproduce the predicted scaling, supporting the theoretical resource-efficiency claims in those settings.
icml-2026-continuous-variable-hamiltonia.tldr: D-RUT converts finite-order quantum Hamiltonian learning into polynomial recovery with proven Heisenberg-limited evolution time and robustness to preparation and measurement errors.

paragraphs: Training a world model across different robots is difficult because their bodies and action spaces differ. An action representation that works for one robot may not connect naturally to another robot’s movements. This paper investigates whether learning a shared internal action space can make experience from diverse robots more useful when adapting to an unseen embodiment.

The proposed LAC-WM conditions its world model on learned latent actions shared across embodiments. The comparison model, EAC-WM, instead uses explicit motion labels. In the reported results, explicit conditioning produces separated action representations across robots, limiting downstream adaptation. The shared latent space provides a common representation through which experience from different embodiments can contribute.

On dexterous manipulation and a modified LIBERO benchmark, LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% and 11.7%, respectively. Its performance also improves as pretraining includes more embodiments, whereas EAC-WM’s declines. These findings suggest that representation choice determines whether greater robot diversity helps or hinders transfer in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-cross-embodiment-robot-foundat.tldr: A shared learned action space helps robot world models transfer to unseen embodiments and benefit from more diverse pretraining.

paragraphs: Structured pruning lowers language-model inference cost by removing architectural components judged less important. One way to select components is to learn gates that control their contribution while constraining how many remain active. Because counting active components creates a discrete optimization problem, earlier methods often introduce randomly sampled, approximately binary gates to make training differentiable.

Deterministic Differentiable Pruning replaces that sampling process with a deterministic, smooth approximation to the sparsity objective. It optimizes the masks alone. This addresses the mismatch between random masks used during training and the fixed choices needed at deployment, while offering more expressive masks than bounded, near-binary alternatives. The authors report faster convergence as well as reduced training-to-deployment mismatch.

The method is evaluated on dense and mixture-of-experts models, including Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. At 20% sparsity it outperforms earlier methods, with downstream performance loss as small as 1% in the reported evaluations. Tests using vLLM also show end-to-end inference speedups, connecting the pruning results to practical deployment benefits.
icml-2026-deterministic-differentiable-s.tldr: DDP learns deterministic pruning masks that reduce model cost while limiting performance loss and delivering measured inference speedups.

paragraphs: Some regular expressions can require disproportionately long matching times, creating opportunities for denial-of-service attacks. Detecting these expressions involves a trade-off: static analysis is efficient but often struggles with features such as lookarounds and backreferences, while methods that execute matches can reduce false alarms at a substantial runtime cost.

RMGNN represents each regular expression as a heterogeneous graph that retains its syntax and extended features. It adds three motifs associated with ReDoS, giving the learning system explicit domain knowledge about relevant structural patterns. Different graph relationships are processed through heterogeneous propagation and kernel-guided motif learning. Residual cross-attention then combines information captured at multiple scales to make a vulnerability prediction.

Across four real-world datasets containing more than 317,000 expressions, RMGNN achieves higher F1-scores than six state-of-the-art baselines. It is also 244 times faster on average than the baseline with the strongest F1-score. These results support using structured graph representations to combine accurate detection with low inference latency.
icml-2026-exploring-motif-based-heteroge.tldr: RMGNN detects vulnerable regular expressions using graph structure and attack-related motifs, improving reported accuracy and inference speed.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models refine tokens over several steps, but written tokens can become irreversible before their underlying decisions are stable. The paper identifies this stability lag as a particular vulnerability during post-training quantization. Small numerical errors can flip borderline choices at the write frontier, after which the mistaken choices remain fixed and their effects can grow.

FAIR-Calib directs calibration effort toward these fragile states. First, it probes a full-precision teacher to estimate which token positions deserve protection, combining how often they encounter the frontier with their reliability during masked stages. It then calibrates individual layers using a weighted hidden-state reconstruction loss. This avoids expensive end-to-end diffusion rollouts while emphasizing errors that matter most near commitment.

The authors theoretically justify the weighted objective as a surrogate for divergence between output distributions. Experiments on LLaDA and Dream with four-bit weights and activations consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines. They also report fewer frontier decision flips and fewer mismatches after commitment, connecting the performance gains to the failure mechanism the method targets.
icml-2026-fair-calib-frontier-aware-inst.tldr: FAIR-Calib protects fragile token decisions during diffusion-language-model quantization by giving their hidden states greater calibration weight.

paragraphs: Merging a vision-language model with a strong reasoning model can improve reasoning without building a new model from scratch. However, merging at the level of whole layers can couple desirable reasoning changes with changes that damage visual perception. FRISM addresses this trade-off by controlling the merge at a finer level within model updates.

The method decomposes reasoning-model task vectors using singular value decomposition. This separates the updates into subspaces whose contributions to reasoning and perception can differ. FRISM learns a scaling coefficient for each subspace, allowing different parts of the update to contribute by different amounts. A label-free self-distillation strategy with two optimization objectives learns these adjustments using common vision-language perception datasets.

Experiments report improved reasoning while largely retaining visual capabilities, with consistently strong results across diverse vision-language reasoning benchmarks. The central finding is that selective control within an update can ease the reasoning–perception trade-off associated with coarser merging. Preservation is substantial rather than claimed to be complete.
icml-2026-frism-fine-grained-reasoning-i.tldr: FRISM selectively merges reasoning-related parameter subspaces into vision-language models, improving reasoning while largely preserving visual capabilities.

paragraphs: Origin–destination modeling describes movement between areas and supports urban planning and mobility analysis. Graph-based approaches can represent connections between locations, but the paper argues that overlooking geographic attributes weakens their handling of long-range relationships and dependencies involving several areas. GeoFlow brings geography directly into both area representations and the processing of relationships between them.

Its encoder combines graph attention for intrinsic area information with coordinate-aware processing for global spatial structure. Representations include relative positions and distance information, including geodesic distances. An axial-global attention decoder then models competitive dependencies specific to origin–destination flows. For generation, the same framework is paired with flow matching to produce varied mobility samples.

The authors report improved predictive accuracy alongside better generative fidelity and diversity. Ablation experiments and analytical studies support the contribution of the individual components. The findings connect geographic representation with both tasks: estimating flows more accurately and generating mobility patterns that better reflect the data while retaining diversity across samples.
icml-2026-geoflow-geo-aware-modeling-of-.tldr: GeoFlow incorporates geographic structure into origin–destination modeling to improve flow prediction and the fidelity and diversity of generated mobility samples.

paragraphs: Exact Cover tasks have known constraints, yet a learning system may still need substantial data to approximate valid solutions. Approaches that combine neural learning with symbolic structure can face their own training and scaling difficulties. HONet aims to exploit the available constraints directly while keeping the overall system trainable end to end.

The architecture combines a deep residual hypergraph encoder with a differentiable quadratic-programming layer whose constraints are fixed. The encoder preserves problem structure, while the optimization layer incorporates the constraint system. Under the paper’s fixed-polytope approach, a geometric consistency loss shapes the learned objective so that a valid discrete solution is encouraged to coincide with the lowest-energy solution. This is an optimization incentive, rather than a stated guarantee for every instance.

Experiments report rapid attainment of 100% accuracy on 9-by-9 Sudoku with limited training samples. HONet also shows stronger data efficiency than the evaluated baselines and robustness in highly sparse regimes and additional tasks. These results support combining learned objectives with explicit constraint structure.
icml-2026-honet-data-efficient-learning-.tldr: HONet combines hypergraph learning with constrained optimization to solve Exact Cover tasks efficiently from limited data.

paragraphs: Answering questions about tables can require more than interpreting a single question and returning one answer. An agent may need to locate relevant tables, choose tools, and respond as the user’s intent changes over several turns. TableAgent-Bench is designed to evaluate this more active setting, which existing single-turn benchmarks largely miss.

The bilingual benchmark contains 1,310 multi-turn dialogues grounded in 2,275 industrial tables. Its construction accounts for table topology and includes structurally complex environments involving multiple tables. The accompanying Table-centric Agent Evaluation Framework provides specialized tools and four categories of metrics. These examine intermediate behavior, including table localization and the appropriateness of tool calls, as well as success across an interaction trajectory.

Evaluating 25 leading agents reveals a substantial capability gap. Even the strongest tested model, Gemini-3-Pro-Preview, reaches only 53.4% information coverage. By examining the steps leading to answers, the framework helps identify where table reasoning breaks down, giving developers a more diagnostic target than final-answer evaluation alone.
icml-2026-how-far-can-llm-agents-reason-.tldr: TableAgent-Bench exposes weaknesses in agents’ multi-turn table reasoning by evaluating table selection, tool use, and interaction trajectories.

paragraphs: A binary judgment that text involved AI can obscure the difference between polishing an existing source and generating new content. The paper argues that confusing these roles creates fairness risks. It therefore focuses on attributing the mode of AI participation, distinguishing editing anchored to source material from generation without such an anchor.

The authors introduce IACW-Instruct, a collection of varied editing operations constructed through a Director–Actor–Judge pipeline. This corpus supports systematic evaluation of the distinction. Their watermarking method, IACW, actively embeds attribution information and uses entropy gating that adapts to intent. The embedding mechanism is designed to preserve meaning while making the type of AI involvement detectable.

Experiments report 95% attribution accuracy after deletion of 20% of the tokens, alongside semantic fidelity close to unwatermarked text. These findings support the feasibility of finer-grained provenance under the tested editing conditions. The attributed distinction concerns source-anchored editing versus unanchored generation, making the role of AI participation more explicit than a simple generated-text label.
icml-2026-iacw-intent-aware-controllable.tldr: IACW embeds intent-sensitive watermarks to distinguish AI editing from generation while maintaining near-unwatermarked semantic fidelity.

paragraphs: Action-conditioned video world models predict future visual observations one step after another. Over long sequences, small errors can accumulate because later predictions depend on earlier generated frames. Existing approaches use pretrained teachers and sequence-level matching to reduce this drift, but add computation and can still suffer error propagation beyond the training horizon.

LIVE introduces a cycle-consistency objective to constrain that accumulation without teacher-based distillation. Starting from ground-truth frames, it generates a forward rollout and then reverses the generation process to reconstruct the initial state. A diffusion loss is applied at the end of this reconstruction cycle. The return path makes the training objective explicitly sensitive to whether extended generation preserves information about where it began.

The paper also presents a unified view of different approaches and a progressive training curriculum for stability. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon benchmarks, with stable, high-quality videos extending well beyond the rollout lengths used in training. These results support cycle consistency as a way to improve extended interactive generation.
icml-2026-live-long-horizon-interactive-.tldr: LIVE uses forward-and-reverse video generation to constrain accumulated error and produce stable sequences beyond its training rollout lengths.

paragraphs: A standard twelve-lead ECG observes the same underlying cardiac electrical activity from several spatial orientations. Learning directly from these signals therefore involves considerable redundancy. The paper argues that this redundancy may encourage spurious correlations and overfitting, making the choice of representation important for tasks ranging from disease diagnosis to clinical report generation.

LVCG moves self-supervised representation learning into a latent vectorcardiogram space motivated by the Frank VCG model. Its aim is to represent the shared electrical activity underlying the measurements. Learning representations that remain consistent across views reduces dependence on artifacts tied to individual leads. The physical interpretation of the latent space provides the organizing principle for this unified representation.

Across the reported tasks, LVCG generally outperforms methods that learn in observable ECG space. The gains include improved robustness and generalization, particularly when the data distribution changes. These findings support representing the common source of multiple ECG views as a useful way to reduce redundancy and improve transfer.
icml-2026-lvcg-learning-ecg-representati.tldr: LVCG learns a shared latent representation of cardiac electrical activity, improving reported robustness and generalization over ECG-space learning.

paragraphs: Designing a multi-agent system involves choosing both how agents connect and what each agent does. Existing automated approaches often couple these decisions, making the resulting structures rigid. MAS-Architect separates topology planning from individual agent implementation so that the system can generate architectures suited to a task from scratch.

The framework uses a code-based declarative representation with a unified interface between these two design concerns. This separation lets collaboration structure be specified independently of the implementation inside each node. A Distill-then-Explore training strategy optimizes the resulting designs. The intended benefit is flexibility in how agents collaborate together with efficiency in the amount of language-model computation they require.

Across five benchmarks, the authors report a new efficiency–performance Pareto frontier relative to the compared methods. The framework achieves 78.7% average accuracy with 2,533 inference tokens per query, surpassing prior methods while substantially reducing token use. Qualitative analysis also finds advanced collaboration patterns emerging autonomously, supporting the flexibility of the declarative design approach.
icml-2026-mas-architect-declarative-mult.tldr: MAS-Architect separates collaboration structure from agent implementation to automatically design more accurate, token-efficient multi-agent systems.

paragraphs: The paper tackles graph combinatorial optimization through a binary quadratic formulation. It uses a classical result to construct a continuous multilinear relaxation that preserves the optimal binary solutions. This removes the need to search only over discrete values, but the continuous objective remains highly nonconvex, with poor local optima that can obstruct optimization.

The authors treat the objective as an energy function and seek solutions by sampling from its associated Boltzmann distribution. They view sampling as moving a simple reference distribution toward this target. Optimal transport then provides a way to characterize efficient probability flow and derive a stochastic control problem whose solution specifies optimal sampling dynamics.

A graph neural network represents the control policy and approximates the optimal control. Experiments report better solution quality and efficiency than strong combinatorial and learning-based baselines. The exactness claim concerns preservation of optimal binary solutions by the relaxation; the implemented sampling control is an approximation. Together, the components connect a principled reformulation with a learned search procedure.
icml-2026-optimal-transportguided-stocha.tldr: The method combines an exact continuous relaxation with optimal-transport-guided learned sampling to improve graph optimization.

paragraphs: Generative-model evaluation becomes expensive when every test requires slow inference or costly rating. ProEval seeks to make each evaluated input more informative while serving two purposes: estimating overall performance and finding failures. It transfers knowledge through pretrained Gaussian processes that approximate how an input maps to a score, such as error severity or a safety-violation metric.

The framework treats performance estimation as Bayesian quadrature, using a probabilistic surrogate to estimate an aggregate score. It treats failure discovery as sampling from regions where scores exceed a threshold. Uncertainty-aware decision strategies select or synthesize inputs for testing, allowing the evaluation budget to focus on cases that help resolve uncertainty or expose failures.

The authors prove unbiasedness and a bound for their pretrained-GP-based estimator. Across reasoning, safety-alignment, and classification benchmarks, ProEval needs 8–65 times fewer samples than competitive baselines to estimate performance within one percentage point of ground truth. It also uncovers more diverse failures under tighter budgets, supporting both efficient measurement and targeted diagnosis.
icml-2026-proeval-proactive-failure-disc.tldr: ProEval uses uncertainty-aware surrogate models to estimate performance with fewer tests while discovering more diverse failures.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can encounter test data that differs from their pretraining data. Test-time adaptation tries to use incoming examples to close that gap. Cache-based methods retain examples for later use, but growing caches increase inference cost, and insufficient or incorrect cached samples can weaken the resulting predictions.

Prototype-Based Test-Time Adaptation accumulates information in class-specific prototypes. Each test example contributes visual features according to its zero-shot class confidence, adaptively controlling its influence on the class representations. Information from earlier examples is retained entirely within these prototypes. This removes the need to populate and retrieve an expanding sample cache while preserving a mechanism for learning from the test stream.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on 15 image-recognition and four robust point-cloud benchmarks. On ten cross-domain benchmarks, CLIP accuracy rises from 65.64% to 69.38%, compared with 67.97% for cache-based TDA. On ImageNet-1K, PTA retains 92% of CLIP’s inference speed, versus TDA’s 50%, illustrating the reported quality–efficiency benefit.
icml-2026-prototype-based-test-time-adap.tldr: PTA adapts vision-language models through confidence-weighted class prototypes, improving accuracy while avoiding sample-cache overhead.

paragraphs: Human preference feedback can be inconsistent or subjective, making it an imperfect training signal for language-model alignment. The paper identifies a problem with treating all preference pairs alike: a disputed comparison can influence training as strongly as one with unanimous agreement. That can encourage a model to fit conflicting judgments and reduce alignment quality.

Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization estimates annotator reliability and infers latent preference labels from noisy feedback. These inferred labels help identify more robust preferences. A reliability-aware consistency objective then changes the training emphasis according to annotation consensus, giving high-agreement supervision greater priority. The inferred labels are part of the method’s estimation process, rather than independently established answers to every subjective comparison.

Experiments on alignment benchmarks report reduced inconsistency and noise in training data and better performance than widely used RLHF baselines. The findings support accounting for the quality and agreement of human feedback when optimizing preferences. The approach makes confidence in supervision part of training instead of assigning every pair equal influence.
icml-2026-reliability-aware-llm-alignmen.tldr: RGPO weights preference learning by annotator reliability and consensus to reduce the impact of inconsistent human feedback.

paragraphs: Watermarks can help identify AI-generated text, but robustness against ordinary editing does not necessarily establish robustness against an adaptive adversary. This paper argues that existing evaluations can overstate security by using insufficiently adversarial tests. It introduces an adaptive robustness radius to formalize worst-case resilience under attacks that adjust to the watermarking problem.

The authors approximate this radius by representing the paraphrase space through a KL-divergence ball. Their analysis shows that optimizing attack context and model parameters can substantially reduce the approximated radius. RLCracker turns this insight into a reinforcement-learning-based paraphrasing attack intended to remove watermark signals while retaining meaning. It uses limited watermarked examples and requires no detector access.

In the reported Unigram-watermark experiment, a three-billion-parameter model trained on 100 short samples achieves 98.5% removal success on 1,500-token texts with minimal semantic shift, compared with 6.75% for GPT-4o. Evaluations span five model sizes and ten watermarking schemes. The findings demonstrate vulnerabilities under adaptive testing, with the headline rate tied to the specified experiment.
icml-2026-rlcracker-evaluating-the-worst.tldr: RLCracker shows that adaptive reinforcement-learning paraphrasing can undermine text watermarks with limited examples and no detector access.

paragraphs: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput by generating rollouts separately from policy updates. The difficulty is that a rollout may come from an older policy. Importance weights used to account for this difference can become heavy-tailed, allowing a few trajectories to dominate the update and sharply increasing policy-gradient variance.

The paper finds that collapsing effective sample size reliably predicts this problem across math, reasoning, and tool-use analyses. VCPO responds in two ways: it adjusts the learning rate according to effective sample size, damping less reliable updates, and uses a closed-form minimum-variance baseline for the off-policy setting. This adds little overhead and does not require a separate critic model.

Experiments report stable asynchronous training across math and general reasoning benchmarks, including rollouts 128 policy steps out of date. In a long-horizon tool-use task, VCPO matches synchronous training performance while reducing training time by a factor of 2.5. The results connect statistical reliability controls with the practical throughput benefits of asynchronous training.
icml-2026-stable-asynchrony-variance-con.tldr: VCPO stabilizes asynchronous language-model reinforcement learning by controlling update variance using effective sample size and an off-policy baseline.

paragraphs: A robot navigating around people must interpret language while reacting to a changing scene. Vision-language reasoning can take much longer than a control update, so its conclusions may describe an earlier situation. TIC-VLA addresses this timing mismatch explicitly, making delayed reasoning part of the action-generation problem rather than assuming reasoning and control are temporally aligned.

Its semantic-control interface combines current observations with delayed vision-language semantic states and information about their latency. The controller therefore receives both the reasoning output and its timing context. Training injects reasoning delays during imitation learning and online reinforcement learning, aligning the learning process with asynchronous deployment. The authors also introduce DynaNav, a physically accurate, photorealistic simulation suite for language-guided navigation in dynamic environments.

Experiments in simulation and on a real robot report consistent improvements over prior vision-language-action models. The system maintains robust real-time control even with reasoning delays lasting multiple seconds. These results support explicitly teaching control policies to act with delayed semantic information while using current observations.
icml-2026-tic-vla-a-think-in-control-vis.tldr: TIC-VLA trains robot controllers to combine current observations with explicitly delayed reasoning, supporting real-time navigation despite multi-second reasoning latency.

paragraphs: Adding chain-of-thought reasoning to robotic vision-language-action models can improve generalization and make their decisions easier to inspect. This paper investigates a security consequence of that design: intermediate reasoning may become a route for redirecting physical actions. The authors first show empirically that reasoning strongly influences action generation even when it conflicts with the user’s instruction.

TRAP targets this reasoning-to-action connection using an adversarial visual patch in the robot’s environment. The patch steers intermediate reasoning toward an attacker-chosen behavior, which can then influence downstream actions without changing the user’s request. This makes the interaction between visual input, generated reasoning, and control central to the attack mechanism.

Evaluations demonstrate effectiveness on three representative reasoning-based VLA models with different reasoning mechanisms. The authors also implement a printed-paper patch in a real-world setting. These results establish the reported vulnerability across multiple tested designs and a physical implementation. They motivate protecting the intermediate reasoning pathway as part of securing robotic action generation.
icml-2026-trap-hijacking-vla-cot-reasoni.tldr: TRAP demonstrates that visual patches can redirect robotic actions by manipulating intermediate reasoning without changing the user’s instruction.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can search for information beyond their internal knowledge, but a small number of image and text queries may not uncover the evidence needed for complex questions. Visual noise makes that assumption especially fragile. Vision-DeepResearch targets questions that require sustained investigation and evidence gathered across several visual and textual sources.

The proposed approach searches over multiple turns, entities, and visual scales. It supports dozens of reasoning steps and hundreds of search-engine interactions, expanding both the depth of investigation and the breadth of evidence collection. Cold-start supervision followed by reinforcement learning trains these research behaviors into the multimodal model itself, producing an end-to-end system.

The authors report substantial improvements over existing multimodal deep-research models and workflows built around GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-pro, and Claude-4-Sonnet. The stated results support training models to conduct extended, varied searches when noisy visual inputs make simple retrieval insufficient. The contribution combines a richer search paradigm with training that develops the model’s ability to use it.
icml-2026-vision-deepresearch-incentiviz.tldr: Vision-DeepResearch trains multimodal models to conduct extended visual and textual investigations across noisy, diverse sources.
